issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Carlos is a 62-year-old Latin American man who has been married for over three decades. He has dedicated his life to dance, performing and teaching in the vibrant arts community of San Francisco. His world was shaken when he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that left him with profound psychological scars. The collision occurred late one evening as Carlos was driving home from a performance. The impact was devastating; he remembers the screeching tires and shattering glass, followed by an overwhelming sense of helplessness as his car spun out of control. The moment he regained consciousness in the hospital, intense shame washed over him, believing it was his fault for not reacting quickly enough. Since then, Carlos has struggled with powerful negative emotions such as fear, horror, and guilt. He feels intense shame whenever he recalls the event, unable to put those feelings into words. This nonverbal memory is compounded by auditory recall; sometimes, in quiet moments, he hears the sounds of his collision echoing through his mind. His negative appraisals have deepened these fears. Carlos believes he will never be able to feel normal emotions again and that bad things are inevitable because of who he is. These beliefs reinforce his sense of helplessness, making him hyper-vigilant about potential threats in everyday situations. He scans for exits whenever he enters a room or building, reacting with alarm when touched unexpectedly. In an effort to cope, Carlos has developed several maladaptive strategies. He deliberately tries to leave his body or blank out during moments that trigger these memories. He often stays up until very late, delaying sleep to avoid the nightmares that haunt him. When these tactics fail, he tries hard not to think about the trauma at all, but this only leads to a cycle of repressed and recurring thoughts. The more Carlos suppresses his memories, the more they resurface with intensity. These intrusive memories often lead to dissociation as he struggles to manage the overwhelming emotions they bring. This pattern has become self-reinforcing: the more he dissociates or avoids sleep, the stronger his negative appraisals and threat perceptions grow. Carlos's occupation as a dancer adds layers of complexity. The physical contact inherent in dance rehearsals is now fraught with anxiety; he reacts defensively to unexpected touches from fellow dancers, which has strained relationships within his community. This tension at work makes him question his ability to perform again and amplifies his belief that something bad will inevitably happen. The cumulative effect of these experiences has left Carlos feeling profoundly isolated. His wife notices a change in his demeanor—more withdrawn and distant—and worries about the impact on their relationship. The realization that he can no longer engage fully in dance, an integral part of his identity, brought him to seek help. What frightens Carlos most is the fear of never regaining his sense of self and the hopelessness he feels about the future. Yet, beneath this fear lies a glimmer of hope that therapy might offer a path back to feeling like himself again—a chance to reconnect with his emotions and find peace from the constant threat of re-experiencing the traumatic event.
